title: Israeli Airstrike Hits Gaza City Apartment, Killing at Least Five Civilians – Al Jazeera Report
body:
A powerful Israeli airstrike that hit a densely populated apartment block in the Remal district of Gaza City on Tuesday left at least five civilians dead and wounded a further six, according to staff at the main medical facility in the enclave. The strike, which came without any prior warning, has ignited fresh outrage among Palestinians and renewed international calls for restraint as the conflict that began in early October enters its seventh week.

The apartment building, located on a narrow street in western Gaza City, was home to several families who had taken refuge there after earlier bombardments reduced much of the city’s housing stock to rubble. Emergency responders who arrived at the scene described a scene of devastation: collapsed walls, shattered windows and a thick plume of dust that lingered over the street. Al‑Shifa Hospital, Gaza’s largest medical centre, received the injured in a critical condition, straining an already overburdened emergency department that has been operating at near‑capacity since the war’s outset.

Israel’s military spokesperson said the strike was aimed at “terror infrastructure” and that the target was a “terrorist command centre” allegedly used by Hamas operatives. The statement did not specify the intelligence that led to the decision, nor did it address the civilian casualties. Human‑rights organisations, including Amnesty International and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights, have called for an independent investigation, arguing that the attack may constitute a breach of international humanitarian law, which obliges parties to a conflict to distinguish between combatants and civilians and to take all feasible precautions to minimise civilian harm.

The incident arrives at a time when the Gaza Strip’s humanitarian situation is deteriorating at an alarming pace. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that more than 80 percent of the enclave’s 2.3 million residents now lack reliable access to clean water, electricity, or medical supplies. Food distribution points are operating at reduced capacity, and the World Health Organization has warned of a looming public‑health crisis as hospitals grapple with shortages of fuel, medicines and staff. The latest civilian deaths underscore the difficulty of delivering aid and protecting non‑combatants in an environment where densely packed residential areas are interwoven with alleged militant sites.

International reactions have been mixed. While the United States reaffirmed its support for Israel’s right to defend itself against rocket fire from Gaza, several European capitals, including Germany and Spain, have urged the Israeli government to exercise greater caution and to adhere to the principles of proportionality and distinction. The United Nations Security Council is expected to convene a special session next week to discuss the escalating civilian toll, though past attempts at a ceasefire have been stymied by deep mistrust on both sides.

Looking ahead, the Remal attack may shape the trajectory of the conflict in several ways. For Hamas and other militant groups, civilian casualties provide potent propaganda material that could bolster recruitment and harden public sentiment against Israel. For the Israeli Defence Forces, the incident could prompt a reassessment of targeting protocols, especially as international scrutiny intensifies and diplomatic pressure mounts. Meanwhile, humanitarian agencies are likely to intensify appeals for safe corridors and ceasefire negotiations to allow the delivery of life‑saving aid. The coming days will reveal whether the tragedy in Remal becomes a catalyst for renewed diplomatic engagement or merely another grim statistic in a war that shows few signs of abating.
